headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Constipation in Pregnancy
headings.content: Constipation is one of the most frequent gastrointestinal complaints during pregnancy, affecting up to forty percent of expectant mothers. Clinically, it is defined by infrequent bowel movements, difficulty during evacuation, or the passage of hard, dry stools. While normal bowel habits vary widely among individuals, a significant drop from one's baseline frequency—often fewer than three bowel movements per week—signals the condition. In Nigerian clinical practice, pregnant women frequently report this discomfort during routine antenatal visits, yet many dismiss it as an inevitable part of gestation rather than a manageable medical issue.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Hormonal Influences
headings.content: The primary driver of slowed bowel motility in pregnancy is the dramatic surge in circulating **progesterone**. This hormone relaxes smooth muscle tissue throughout the body, including the gastrointestinal tract, which significantly prolongs transit time. As food moves more sluggishly through the intestines, the colon has extra time to absorb water from the stool, resulting in the characteristic hard consistency. Additionally, as the uterus enlarges during the second and third trimesters, mechanical compression on the bowel physically impedes normal peristalsis and evacuation.

headings.title: Contributing Factors and Antenatal Triggers
headings.content:
- **Iron Supplementation**: Routine antenatal iron tablets prescribed to prevent anaemia frequently cause dark, firm stools and constipation.
- **Dietary Shifts**: Reduced intake of fibrous local foods, such as vegetables, beans, and whole grains, diminishes stool bulk.
- **Fluid Deficient Intake**: Inadequate water consumption, especially in hot tropical climates, worsens stool hardening.
- **Reduced Physical Activity**: A sedentary lifestyle or decreased ambulation slows overall metabolic and gastrointestinal function.

headings.title: Clinical Presentation and Assessment
headings.content: Thorough nursing assessment involves asking targeted questions about bowel habits, stool consistency, straining effort, and abdominal discomfort. Nurses should check for associated symptoms like bloating, flatulence, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. Abdominal palpation may reveal mild tenderness or palpable stool masses in the lower quadrants. It is vital to screen for warning signs such as rectal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or unexplained weight loss, which necessitate prompt medical referral to rule out more serious pathologies like bowel obstruction or fissures.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Associated Risks
headings.content: Left unmanaged, chronic constipation can lead to painful secondary conditions. The most common of these is the development or exacerbation of **hemorrhoids**, caused by increased venous pressure during straining and pelvic congestion. Straining can also cause anal fissures, producing sharp pain and minor bleeding during defecation. In severe cases, fecal impaction may occur, leading to obstipation, paradoxical diarrhea, or even urinary retention due to mechanical pressure on the bladder from the impacted rectal vault.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Nursing Interventions
headings.content: First-line management always centers on safe, lifestyle-based modifications. Nurses should counsel patients to gradually increase dietary fiber intake using locally available foods such as pawpaw, mangoes, garden eggs, beans, and whole grains. Adequate hydration is equally critical; encouraging regular water consumption throughout the day helps soften stool bulk. Safe, moderate physical activity—such as brisk daily walking—stimulates peristalsis. Finally, advising patients to establish a consistent toileting routine without ignoring the natural urge to defecate prevents further rectal desensitization.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Safe Use of Laxatives
headings.content: When lifestyle adjustments fail to bring relief, healthcare providers may introduce pharmacological agents. **Bulk-forming laxatives** like psyllium husk are generally considered the safest medical choice because they mimic natural dietary fiber and are not systemically absorbed. **Osmotic laxatives**, such as polyethylene glycol or lactulose, draw water into the stool and are also widely accepted as safe. Conversely, stimulant laxatives should be used with caution and only for short durations to prevent uterine irritability or electrolyte imbalance. Castor oil must be strictly avoided as it can trigger premature uterine contractions.

headings.title: Patient Education and Preventive Nursing Care
headings.content: Comprehensive patient education empowers expectant mothers to take charge of their digestive health during antenatal care. Nurses must explain the rationale behind iron supplementation and how to counterbalance its constipating effects with increased fluids and high-fiber local nutrition. Teaching proper posture during defecation—such as using a small footstool to elevate the knees—can also align the anorectal angle for easier evacuation. By reinforcing these preventive habits at every clinic visit, nurses significantly reduce the incidence of painful pregnancy-related bowel complications.
